narrativeReportMd:
# MedicinalProductAuthorization R4-to-R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
R4 `MedicinalProductAuthorization` does not survive as the same R6 resource. The best local successor is R6 `RegulatedAuthorization`, but the resource type, canonical URL, subject domain, several field names, and several regulatory data slots changed. Existing R4 instances are not directly valid R6 instances and need an explicit migration transform.

## Scope
The assessment compared the R4 StructureDefinition with the inferred R6 successor `RegulatedAuthorization`, plus local package indexes and supporting R6 terminology artifacts. Inherited base-resource changes are excluded.

## Main migration themes
The main themes are resource identity replacement, element renaming or merging, loss of several R4 marketing-authorization-specific dates, and a broader R6 authorization model that supports non-medicinal subjects. Some mappings are straightforward, such as `identifier`, `holder`, `regulator`, `statusDate`, and `validityPeriod`; others are lossy or require policy decisions.

## Highest-impact findings
The highest-impact issue is the missing R6 `MedicinalProductAuthorization` resource identity. Additional high-impact issues are the removed marketing-authorization date fields, the removal or relocation of `jurisdictionalAuthorization`, and the changed subject target domain.

## Findings requiring human review
Human review is needed for counterpart confirmation, lossy field migrations, legal status of supply relocation, and terminology choices for the new R6 preferred/example bindings.

## Backward-compatible design observations
Many changes could have been made less disruptive by preserving an alias resource, keeping old elements deprecated, or adding optional successor elements beside old fields. The R6 design appears to favor a more general authorization model over wire compatibility.

## Follow-up analysis
Review `RegulatedAuthorization`, `MedicinalProductDefinition`, `PackagedProductDefinition`, relevant regulated-authorization ValueSets, and any official R4-to-R6 maps if available.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: `MedicinalProductAuthorization` is effectively removed or renamed in R6, with `RegulatedAuthorization` as the inferred successor. The top migration concerns are resource identity replacement, lossy handling of old marketing-authorization-specific dates and jurisdictional authorizations, and broader R6 subject/content that cannot round-trip to R4. The main uncertainty is the absence of an official cross-version map or narrative rationale.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Migration should start with a resource-level transform to `RegulatedAuthorization`, then map stable elements (`identifier`, `holder`, `regulator`, `status`, `statusDate`, `validityPeriod`) and handle renamed concepts (`country`/`jurisdiction` to `region`, `legalBasis` to `basis`, `procedure` to `case`). Removed R4 fields require extensions, companion resources, or manual policy. R6 content that uses non-medicinal subjects or new documentation/indication/intended-use fields is not cleanly representable in R4.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high that the old R4 resource is absent in R6 and that `RegulatedAuthorization` is the closest local successor. Confidence is medium for detailed migration semantics because no official diff, ConceptMap, StructureMap, terminology expansion, or narrative ballot page was available.

findings.title: R4 MedicinalProductAuthorization is absent in R6 and replaced by inferred successor RegulatedAuthorization

oldState.summary: Concrete R4 resource type and canonical StructureDefinition exist.

semanticText.definition: The regulatory authorization of a medicinal product.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 has a concrete `MedicinalProductAuthorization` resource with resourceType `MedicinalProductAuthorization` and canonical URL `http://hl7.org/fhir/StructureDefinition/MedicinalProductAuthorization`.

newState.summary: No R6 StructureDefinition with the old name; closest local successor is RegulatedAuthorization.

semanticText.definition: Regulatory approval, clearance or licensing related to a regulated product, treatment, facility or activity that is cited in a guidance, regulation, rule or legislative act. An example is Market Authorization relating to a Medicinal Product.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 has no `StructureDefinition-MedicinalProductAuthorization.json`. The R6 package lists `MedicinalProductAuthorization` in `fhir-old-types` and defines `RegulatedAuthorization` as the active resource whose scope includes medicinal-product market authorization.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: `RegulatedAuthorization` is the only R6 resource StructureDefinition with authorization semantics in the local package, and its definition explicitly includes market authorization for medicinal products.

impact.impactRationaleMd: A conformant R6 validator will not accept an instance whose `resourceType` is `MedicinalProductAuthorization` because that resource type is no longer defined as a concrete R6 resource. Generated R4 classes, REST endpoint routing, search parameter names, and type switches all need migration to `RegulatedAuthorization` or another local policy. In the reverse direction, generic R6 `RegulatedAuthorization` content may represent authorizations beyond medicinal products and cannot be safely downcast to the R4 resource.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Marketing authorization records are regulatory business records. Misrouting or silently dropping them during resource-type migration can affect licensing, market status, and compliance workflows.

justification.inferredGoal: Generalize medicinal product authorization into a broader regulated authorization model.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain `MedicinalProductAuthorization` as a deprecated concrete compatibility resource while adding `RegulatedAuthorization`.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred R6 goal--a broader `RegulatedAuthorization` resource that can cover products, facilities, activities, and other regulated subjects--is reasonable. A compatibility resource could have reduced R4-to-R6 wire breakage, but maintaining two concrete base resources for the same medicinal market authorization fact would be a material interoperability and governance cost. On balance, the resource-identity break is probably justified, although not the only possible design.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best less-breaking base design would be to keep `MedicinalProductAuthorization` in R6 as a deprecated concrete specialization or compatibility resource, not merely as conversion guidance. That would allow most R4 instances and resource-type dispatch to continue while new implementations used `RegulatedAuthorization`. The cost is a persistent dual representation: systems could indefinitely create either resource for the same authorization, with duplicated endpoint, search, canonical, and conformance expectations.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves old resourceType values, but creates duplicate resource identities, endpoints, canonical URLs, search surfaces, and long-lived ambiguity for the same medicinal authorization.

evidence.detail: R4 defines the MedicinalProductAuthorization StructureDefinition.
R6 RegulatedAuthorization covers market authorization for medicinal products.
evidence.quote: An example is Market Authorization relating to a Medicinal Product.

evidence.sourceRef: R6 package index and file system
evidence.detail: The assigned R6 StructureDefinition file is absent.
R6 lists MedicinalProductAuthorization as an old resource name no longer used in this FHIR version.

examples.examplesMd: The examples are illustrative fragments focused on the resource identity and not full regulatory records.

findings.narrativeMd: `MedicinalProductAuthorization` is not a same-name R6 resource. This is a hard wire-format break: old instances, generated classes, REST resource-type routes, and resource-type switch statements must move to a new resource identity. The local evidence strongly points to `RegulatedAuthorization` as the successor, but the successor is broader than the old medicinal-product-only resource.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4 instance with `resourceType: MedicinalProductAuthorization` is old-valid but R6-invalid because no R6 StructureDefinition defines that resource type. Conversely, an R6 `RegulatedAuthorization` can authorize products, facilities, activities, or research artifacts, so not every R6 instance is representable as R4 `MedicinalProductAuthorization`.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Create an explicit resource-level transform. At minimum, rewrite `resourceType`, update canonical/profile references, update endpoint and type dispatch logic, and then apply element-level mappings described in the other findings. Do not rely on tolerant parsing or type aliases unless a local compatibility layer deliberately provides them.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change probably supports a broader regulatory model, but a compatibility alias, deprecated resource, or official profile over `RegulatedAuthorization` could have reduced instance breakage. The tradeoff would be additional maintenance and possible ambiguity about whether old medicinal-only semantics or new generalized semantics apply.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Because no official ConceptMap or narrative migration note was available, the `RegulatedAuthorization` successor relationship is inferred rather than proven by an authoritative map.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R6 has no same-name `MedicinalProductAuthorization` resource, and local evidence strongly supports `RegulatedAuthorization` as the intended successor. This is a real top-level wire/API break because old `resourceType`, canonical/profile references, REST routes, generated classes, and type dispatch do not carry forward unchanged. Still, the R4 resource was FMM 0/trial-use and the R6 successor deliberately generalizes authorization beyond medicinal products. Keeping both concrete resource identities would preserve old payloads but would create durable duplicate endpoints and canonical types for the same marketing-authorization fact, so the break looks proportionate rather than a standards issue that clearly needs reopening.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition defines concrete resource `MedicinalProductAuthorization` with FMM 0/trial-use.
R6 package has no `StructureDefinition-MedicinalProductAuthorization.json`.
R6 `CodeSystem/fhir-old-types` describes old resource names as deleted or renamed and includes `MedicinalProductAuthorization`.
R6 `RegulatedAuthorization` definition explicitly includes market authorization for a medicinal product as an example.

Lightweight web search found public HL7 Europe/UNICOM IDMP material using `RegulatedAuthorization` for marketing authorization, suggesting implementation relevance but not proving broad R4 production deployment.
freshReview.fmmEffect: R4 FMM 0 and trial-use substantially soften the stability objection to a resource identity replacement. The regulatory domain keeps the migration important, but low FMM prevents treating the break alone as disproportionate.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: an R4 instance with `resourceType: MedicinalProductAuthorization` is not a base R6 instance, and runtime/API/codegen surfaces tied to the old resource type also change.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: A less-breaking base design could have kept `MedicinalProductAuthorization` as a deprecated compatibility resource, but that would maintain two concrete resource identities and likely duplicate endpoint, search, profile, and mapping obligations. That alternative is real but costly.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing high-impact assessment and partial alternative: the technical break is real, but FMM 0 and the high cost of dual resource identities make `Breaking but probably OK` more appropriate than escalation.

findings.title: subject changes from a single medicinal product/package reference to a repeatable broad authorization subject

oldState.summary: Optional single Reference to MedicinalProduct or MedicinalProductPackaged.

semanticText.definition: The medicinal product that is being authorized.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 `subject` identifies at most one authorized medicinal product or packaged medicinal product.

newState.summary: Repeatable Reference to many regulated subject types, including renamed product-definition resources and non-medicinal resources.

semanticText.definition: The product type, treatment, facility or activity that is being authorized.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 `subject` is broader and repeatable, reflecting the generalized `RegulatedAuthorization` resource.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element name and role match, but the resource target universe changed with the R6 model.

impact.impactRationaleMd: After resource-level migration, an R4 reference such as `MedicinalProduct/123` must be retargeted to the R6 product-definition resource identity. Validators that enforce reference target profiles can reject old target resource types. R6 instances can also have multiple subjects or non-medicinal subjects, which cannot be represented in the single medicinal-product/package slot available in R4.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Incorrect subject migration can attach an authorization to the wrong regulated product or activity.

justification.inferredGoal: Allow one authorization resource to cover many regulated subject categories.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Broaden `subject` while also allowing old `MedicinalProduct` and `MedicinalProductPackaged` targets through retained compatibility product resources.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The broader `subject` target list is aligned with the generalized authorization model, and the old target resources were themselves replaced by product-definition resources. A less-breaking design is plausible only if R6 also retained the old product resource identities or aliases. That cross-resource duplication and target-profile ambiguity is material, so the breaking target replacement is probably justified.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base R6 design could have made `RegulatedAuthorization.subject` additive by retaining the old medicinal product/package target profiles alongside the new broader targets. This would not be just migration guidance; it would require base R6 compatibility definitions for the old target resources. The tradeoff is substantial because product data could then be represented through old and new resource identities, making validation, references, and long-term convergence harder.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Would preserve many old references, but depends on cross-artifact compatibility aliases and creates duplicate medicinal product and packaged product identities.

evidence.detail: R4 subject cardinality is 0..1 and targets MedicinalProduct or MedicinalProductPackaged.
R6 subject cardinality is 0..* and targets a broad list including MedicinalProductDefinition, PackagedProductDefinition, and non-medicinal resources.

examples.examplesMd: The old-valid/new-invalid fragment assumes the resource has already been renamed to `RegulatedAuthorization` but still carries an old target resource type.

findings.narrativeMd: `subject` keeps the same broad role but changes substantially. Old medicinal-product references must be retargeted to R6 product-definition resource identities, while R6 can express multiple or non-medicinal subjects that R4 could not carry.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4-to-R6 validation risk is potential rather than absolute because some validators do not resolve references deeply, but target-profile-aware validation and generated reference helpers can reject old targets. R6-to-R4 risk is high because multiplicity and target domains exceed the R4 element.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Build subject migration together with the resource migration for `MedicinalProduct` and `MedicinalProductPackaged`. Reject, split, or extension-map R6 authorizations with multiple or non-medicinal subjects when producing R4.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The broadening fits the generalized resource, but preserving a medicinal-specific alias or profile would have given implementers a safer migration bridge. The tradeoff is additional complexity and possible duplication with product-definition resource changes.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Target resource migration depends on separate analyses for `MedicinalProduct`, `MedicinalProductPackaged`, `MedicinalProductDefinition`, and `PackagedProductDefinition`.

freshReview.narrativeMd: `subject` changes from one reference to old medicinal-product resource identities into a repeatable reference that can point to many regulated subjects, including R6 product-definition resources and non-medicinal subjects. Forward migration needs retargeting when validators or code enforce target profiles; reverse migration can be lossy for multiple or non-medicinal subjects. The broadening is central to the generalized `RegulatedAuthorization` model, and preserving old targets would depend on retaining the old product resource identities too, so the compatibility cost appears justified.
keyEvidence: R4 `MedicinalProductAuthorization.subject` is 0..1 Reference to `MedicinalProduct` or `MedicinalProductPackaged`.
R6 `RegulatedAuthorization.subject` is 0..* Reference to `MedicinalProductDefinition`, `PackagedProductDefinition`, and many other regulated subject types.
R6 `fhir-old-types` includes the old medicinal product resource names, so old target identities are not simply retained as ordinary R6 resources.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 0/trial-use lowers the expectation that R6 must preserve the exact R4 subject target universe. The path is important for regulatory meaning, so the risk remains real, but not enough to outweigh the broader R6 design goal.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: after resource migration, old target resource types can fail target-profile-aware validation or generated-reference constraints; R6-to-R4 loss also occurs for multiple or non-medicinal subjects.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: The less-breaking option would be to keep old `MedicinalProduct` and `MedicinalProductPackaged` targets alongside the new target list. That is only partially attractive because it requires cross-resource compatibility aliases and leaves two product models active.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree: the existing report correctly identifies high reverse-conversion risk and a partial alternative, but the low maturity and cross-artifact cost make the break probably acceptable.

findings.title: country and jurisdiction are replaced or merged into region

oldState.summary: Separate repeatable CodeableConcept elements for country and jurisdiction.

semanticText.definition: Country of marketing authorization and jurisdiction within a country were separate top-level concepts.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 had `country` for the country where marketing authorization was granted and `jurisdiction` for jurisdiction within a country.

semanticText.definition: The territory, e.g. country or jurisdiction, in which the authorization has been granted.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 uses `region` to represent the territory in which the authorization has been granted.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The definitions overlap around territory of authorization, but the old country-vs-jurisdiction distinction is no longer represented by two separate top-level fields.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The old element names are not valid R6 `RegulatedAuthorization` elements, so migrated instances must rename or merge them. The mapping is usually straightforward for simple country codes, but it can be lossy when R4 intentionally distinguished country from sub-country jurisdiction.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Territory is a core regulatory dimension; losing the distinction can affect authorization applicability.

justification.inferredGoal: Use a more general territory element for all regulated authorizations.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep optional `country` and `jurisdiction` in the base resource with clarified territory semantics, adding `region` only if needed for genuinely new R6 cases.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: A generalized territory concept is reasonable, but replacing two optional R4 fields with a new `region` field was not necessary to meet that goal. R6 could have preserved old instances by continuing to accept `country` and `jurisdiction`, with clearer definitions or profile guidance for broader regulated-authorization use cases. The compatibility tradeoff is modest compared with forcing every old payload to rename or merge territory data.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The strongest alternative is to retain `country` and `jurisdiction` as base R6 elements and clarify that together they identify the authorization territory. If broader R6 use cases need a more neutral label, `region` could be added with explicit precedence rules, but the old fields should still be accepted. This preserves R4-valid instances while meeting the main semantic goal, with the main risk being some nonuniform terminology and possible duplicate territory capture if implementers use both old and new fields.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Old names are less uniform than `region`; if `region` is also added, guidance is needed to avoid conflicting territory fields.

evidence.detail: R4 defines separate repeatable country and jurisdiction elements.
R6 defines a repeatable region element bound by example to jurisdiction codes.

examples.examplesMd: The example shows a likely transform after resource renaming; it is not claiming that country and jurisdiction are always semantically interchangeable.

findings.narrativeMd: R4 split authorization territory into `country` and `jurisdiction`. R6 collapses this into `region`. That simplifies the generalized model but removes a structural distinction that old code and data may depend on.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 elements named `country` and `jurisdiction` are not valid on R6 `RegulatedAuthorization`. R6 `region` can often be mapped back to R4, but without additional coding policy it may be unclear whether a region should become `country`, `jurisdiction`, or both.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Map country-level codings to `region`. Preserve sub-country or regulator-specific jurisdiction distinctions using coding systems where possible. For R6-to-R4 conversion, define deterministic rules for separating country from other jurisdictional regions.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A backward-compatible alternative was available: retain old fields and add `region`. The R6 choice avoids duplicate fields but makes old instances fail without transformation.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 separated authorization territory into repeatable `country` and `jurisdiction`; R6 replaces those old wire names with repeatable `region`. This is an old-valid/new-invalid element-name break, and the old distinction can matter when a marketing authorization is country-level but has sub-country or regulator-specific jurisdictional detail. Because these were optional CodeableConcept fields, R6 could likely have kept the old fields or kept one of the old names while clarifying broader territory semantics. The generalized `region` name is cleaner, but the cost of a less-breaking base design appears modest.
keyEvidence: R4 `country` and `jurisdiction` are separate 0..* CodeableConcept elements.
R6 `RegulatedAuthorization.region` is a single 0..* CodeableConcept with definition covering country or jurisdiction.
R6 `region` has only an example jurisdiction binding, so terminology binding does not itself force a hard validation break.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 0/trial-use softens the stability concern, but territorial applicability is a core regulatory/audit dimension. That domain importance and the modest compatibility alternative support `Revisit` despite low maturity.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: old `country` and `jurisdiction` element names are not valid R6 `RegulatedAuthorization` elements; R6-to-R4 loss can occur when a `region` cannot be deterministically classified back into country versus jurisdiction.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Yes. R6 could have retained `country` and `jurisdiction` as optional elements, perhaps deprecating them or defining them as territory components, while adding `region` only if needed. The tradeoff is duplicate or overlapping territory fields, but precedence rules are manageable.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree with the existing medium-impact and less-breaking-available assessment; the change is a real avoidable wire break on a central regulatory path.

findings.title: marketing-authorization-specific date and exclusivity fields are removed from the successor

oldState.summary: R4 has dedicated date/period fields for restoration, data exclusivity, first authorization, and international birth date.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 separately represented `restoreDate`, `dataExclusivityPeriod`, `dateOfFirstAuthorization`, and `internationalBirthDate` as summary elements.

newState.summary: R6 RegulatedAuthorization has no direct counterparts for these fields.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 keeps `statusDate` and `validityPeriod`, but no local `RegulatedAuthorization` elements directly preserve anticipated restoration date, data exclusivity period, first authorization date, or international birth date.

facts.newValue: RegulatedAuthorization.validityPeriod.start, only if local policy treats it as the authorization start

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: Searches of the R6 RegulatedAuthorization, MedicinalProductDefinition, and PackagedProductDefinition StructureDefinitions did not find direct local counterparts for these date concepts.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 instances containing any of these fields cannot be represented directly on R6 `RegulatedAuthorization`. Dropping them would be lossy and can alter regulatory meaning. Some dates might be approximated by `validityPeriod` or `case.date[x]`, but the definitions are not equivalent.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Data exclusivity and authorization dates can drive market-entry, generic submission, renewal, and compliance decisions.

justification.inferredGoal: Remove medicinal-product-specific fields from a generalized authorization resource.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain the optional marketing-authorization date and exclusivity fields in base `RegulatedAuthorization` for medicinal-product authorization use cases.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Removing medicinal-specific date fields helps keep `RegulatedAuthorization` generic, but the local R6 definitions do not show a direct replacement for restoration date, data exclusivity period, first authorization date, or international birth date. Because these fields were optional, retaining them would have preserved R4 instances and important regulatory facts with only moderate base-resource clutter. The break therefore looks probably avoidable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The base-design alternative is to keep these fields, perhaps marked deprecated or limited by definition to medicinal product market authorizations, while the rest of `RegulatedAuthorization` supports broader authorization domains. Official extensions or conversion tooling could mitigate migration, but they are not the core backward-compatible alternative. Keeping optional base elements would preserve old data without requiring lossy extensions or local policy for common regulatory lifecycle facts.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Adds medicinal-product-specific optional content to a generalized resource, but avoids losing high-value regulatory dates and creates little duplicate same-resource representation.

evidence.detail: R4 defines four dedicated date/period elements for marketing authorization lifecycle and exclusivity.
R6 RegulatedAuthorization has statusDate and validityPeriod but no direct elements for restoreDate, dataExclusivityPeriod, dateOfFirstAuthorization, or internationalBirthDate.

evidence.locator: text search of local element definitions
evidence.detail: Related R6 product-definition resources did not reveal direct counterparts for data exclusivity, first authorization, restoration date, or international birth date.

examples.examplesMd: The migration example uses a placeholder extension URL to show the likely need for an extension or profile-specific rule; it is not an HL7-defined extension.

findings.narrativeMd: R4 carried several marketing-authorization-specific dates directly on the resource. R6 `RegulatedAuthorization` does not. These are not just cosmetic fields: they often encode regulatory lifecycle and exclusivity facts.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: After resource renaming, an instance that keeps these old element names is R6-invalid. If a migration drops them, the instance may validate but no longer preserves the R4 business facts. R6-to-R4 is not the main issue for these removed fields; the larger risk is R4 data loss during forward migration.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Inventory usage of these elements before migration. Use official extensions or local profiles if available; otherwise create governed extensions or map a narrowly defined subset, such as first authorization date to `validityPeriod.start`, only when business owners confirm equivalence. Include regression tests for each removed field.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The removal was avoidable from a wire-compatibility perspective because optional elements could have remained in the successor or been preserved through official extensions. The tradeoff would be a less generic base `RegulatedAuthorization` resource.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Human review should confirm whether R6 narrative guidance places these facts in another resource or extension not evident from the local StructureDefinitions.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 had dedicated slots for `restoreDate`, `dataExclusivityPeriod`, `dateOfFirstAuthorization`, and `internationalBirthDate`. R6 `RegulatedAuthorization` keeps `statusDate` and `validityPeriod`, but those do not fully preserve the removed medicinal-product authorization lifecycle and exclusivity facts. Some first-authorization semantics might be approximated by `validityPeriod.start`, but data exclusivity and international birth date are distinct regulatory concepts. Dropping or extension-mapping these fields can require expert policy judgment and can affect compliance, market-entry, and audit workflows.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition defines `restoreDate`, `dataExclusivityPeriod`, `dateOfFirstAuthorization`, and `internationalBirthDate` as optional summary elements.
R6 `RegulatedAuthorization` contains `statusDate` and `validityPeriod` but no direct elements with those names or definitions.
Targeted local search of R6 `RegulatedAuthorization`, `MedicinalProductDefinition`, and `PackagedProductDefinition` found no direct counterpart for these four removed fields.
freshReview.fmmEffect: The low FMM reduces reliance expectations for the R4 shape, but these dates are regulatory/business/audit relevant and migration is lossy or policy-dependent. That overcomes the low-maturity softening.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: old element names are invalid after migration to R6; R4-to-R6 loss is also likely if the values are dropped or squeezed into non-equivalent date fields.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Yes. R6 could have retained these optional fields on `RegulatedAuthorization`, marked them medicinal-product-specific or deprecated, or introduced equivalent optional lifecycle-date elements. The tradeoff is some medicinal-product-specific clutter in a generalized resource, but it would preserve important facts with limited structural cost.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree with the existing high-impact and less-breaking-available assessment; this is one of the strongest findings for renewed design review.

findings.title: jurisdictionalAuthorization backbone is removed or split across other R6 concepts

oldState.summary: Repeatable backbone for authorization in areas within a country.

semanticText.definition: Authorization in areas within a country.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 `jurisdictionalAuthorization` included identifier, country, jurisdiction, legalStatusOfSupply, and validityPeriod.

newState.summary: No equivalent backbone on RegulatedAuthorization; some legal status concepts appear on product-definition resources.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 `RegulatedAuthorization` has top-level `region` and `validityPeriod`, but no nested jurisdictional authorization backbone. Related R6 product resources define `legalStatusOfSupply`, suggesting at least partial relocation outside this resource.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: No one R6 element preserves the old nested structure; related concepts are distributed across the successor resource and product-definition resources.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Old instances with jurisdiction-specific authorizations cannot be migrated by simple renaming. Multiple nested authorizations may require multiple R6 resources, product-definition updates, extensions, or loss of legal-status detail. Reverse conversion is also ambiguous because R6 product legal-status data may not identify the same authorization-specific grouping.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Jurisdiction-specific supply status and validity can determine whether a product may be supplied in a region.

justification.inferredGoal: Move jurisdictional and product supply details out of a generalized authorization resource.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain an optional `jurisdictionalAuthorization` backbone, or an equivalent base backbone, for jurisdiction-specific authorization rows.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The apparent R6 goal of normalizing territory, validity, and legal-supply data across authorization and product-definition resources is reasonable. However, no single R6 element shown in the local definitions preserves the old composite jurisdictional authorization record, including identifiers, jurisdiction, legal status of supply, and validity as one grouped row. Retaining the optional backbone would have preserved R4-valid instances with manageable conformance guidance, so the removal appears probably avoidable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base R6 design could retain `jurisdictionalAuthorization` as an optional deprecated backbone on `RegulatedAuthorization`, even if new modeling guidance encourages use of top-level `region`, `validityPeriod`, or product-definition legal status where appropriate. This is more than migration tooling because the base R6 resource would still accept old data. The tradeoff is possible overlap and conflict rules, but the old backbone carries a grouped fact that the successor model does not cleanly replace.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Some overlap with `region`, `validityPeriod`, and product legal-status modeling would need rules, but preserving the composite backbone avoids lossy multi-resource migration.

evidence.detail: R4 defines the jurisdictionalAuthorization backbone and five local children.
R6 RegulatedAuthorization has no jurisdictionalAuthorization backbone or legalStatusOfSupply child.
R6 product-definition resources include legalStatusOfSupply elements, indicating possible relocation of part of the R4 backbone outside RegulatedAuthorization.

examples.examplesMd: The migration example intentionally omits legal status of supply because the local successor does not have an equivalent slot; product-definition update or extension would be needed.

findings.narrativeMd: `jurisdictionalAuthorization` is one of the largest local content-model changes. R4 grouped jurisdiction, identifier, validity, and legal supply status together. R6 does not preserve that group on `RegulatedAuthorization`, and legal supply status appears to have moved toward product-definition resources.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Keeping the old backbone after resource renaming makes the instance R6-invalid. Flattening it into `region` and `validityPeriod` can validate but loses grouping and legal-status data. R6-to-R4 reconstruction is uncertain because relevant data may live outside `RegulatedAuthorization`.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Do not flatten jurisdictional authorizations without business review. Decide whether each R4 backbone row becomes a separate `RegulatedAuthorization`, an update to `MedicinalProductDefinition` or `PackagedProductDefinition`, a governed extension, or a combination. Test cases should include multiple jurisdictional authorizations with different validity periods and supply statuses.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change could have been less disruptive with a deprecated backbone or official extension. The likely benefit of the R6 design is normalization across authorization and product-definition resources, but the cost is a non-local migration.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Confirm with official R6 guidance whether legal status of supply is intended to be migrated only to product-definition resources.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 `jurisdictionalAuthorization` grouped identifier, country, jurisdiction, legal status of supply, and validity period into repeatable jurisdiction-specific authorization rows. R6 `RegulatedAuthorization` has top-level `region` and `validityPeriod`, while legal status of supply appears on related product-definition resources rather than as the same grouped authorization fact. A simple flattening can lose grouping and legal-status context, and a faithful migration may require multiple resources or governed extensions. This is more than a cosmetic refactor.
keyEvidence: R4 `jurisdictionalAuthorization` is 0..* BackboneElement with `identifier`, `country`, `jurisdiction`, `legalStatusOfSupply`, and `validityPeriod` children.
R6 `RegulatedAuthorization` has no `jurisdictionalAuthorization` or `legalStatusOfSupply` child.

R6 `MedicinalProductDefinition.legalStatusOfSupply` and `PackagedProductDefinition.legalStatusOfSupply` exist, indicating possible relocation outside the authorization resource but not preserving the same grouped row.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 0/trial-use lowers stability pressure, but jurisdiction-specific supply status and validity are regulatory and audit relevant, and the migration is non-local and lossy enough to warrant revisiting.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: the old backbone is invalid in R6; R4-to-R6 loss can occur if grouped jurisdictional authorization rows are flattened or moved into separate product-definition data without preserving relationships.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Yes. R6 could have retained the optional backbone, possibly deprecated or constrained to medicinal-product authorizations, while recommending newer normalized modeling. The tradeoff is overlap with `region`, `validityPeriod`, and product legal-status elements, but the old grouped fact has no clean base replacement.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree with the existing high-impact and less-breaking-available assessment; the fresh review confirms the migration is lossy and expert-dependent.

findings.title: procedure backbone is renamed to case with changed child rules

oldState.summary: Optional single procedure backbone with identifier 0..1, required type 1..1, date[x] 0..1, and recursive application 0..*.

semanticText.definition: The regulatory procedure for granting or amending a marketing authorization.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 models the regulatory process as `procedure`; if present, `procedure.type` is mandatory.

newState.summary: Optional single case backbone with identifier 0..*, type 0..1, status 0..1, date[x] 0..1, and recursive application 0..*.

semanticText.definition: The case or regulatory procedure for granting or amending a regulated authorization.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 models the process as `case`, adds `case.status`, allows multiple identifiers, and no longer requires `case.type` when the backbone is present.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: Definitions and recursive application structures indicate `case` is the successor to R4 `procedure`, but it is not structurally identical.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The old `procedure` property name is not valid in R6. R4-to-R6 migration is usually possible by renaming `procedure` to `case`, but R6 allows cases without a type and with multiple identifiers plus status, which cannot be represented losslessly in the R4 backbone.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The procedure/case can capture regulatory submissions and amendments; loss of status or identifiers can affect auditability.

justification.inferredGoal: Use broader case terminology for generalized regulated authorization workflows.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep the `procedure` element name while broadening its definition and child rules to cover R6 case semantics.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 goal of modeling a broader administrative case is reasonable, and adding case status, multiple identifiers, or relaxed child cardinalities is mostly additive or weakening for forward migration. The hard R4-to-R6 break is primarily the field rename. Because R6 could have kept the nonoptimal `procedure` name with clearer definitions and expanded children, this rename was probably avoidable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best base alternative is not to add both `procedure` and `case`, which would create duplicate workflow fields, but to retain `procedure` and redefine it as the regulatory procedure or administrative case for an authorization. New children such as status could be added under the old backbone, and `procedure.type` could be relaxed. This preserves old instances while meeting the broader modeling goal at the cost of retaining a less general name.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: The old name is less ideal for generalized regulatory cases, but avoids a field-name break and avoids duplicate `procedure`/`case` representations.

evidence.detail: R4 defines the procedure backbone and children.
R6 defines the case backbone and children, including case.status.

examples.examplesMd: FHIR JSON choice serialization uses `dateDateTime` for a `date[x]` value of type dateTime.

findings.narrativeMd: The regulatory workflow backbone is not simply carried forward under the same name. `procedure` becomes `case`, and the child rules are relaxed or expanded. This affects generated models and hand-written JSON transforms.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An old `procedure` element is invalid on R6 `RegulatedAuthorization`. An R6 `case` without `type` cannot be represented as an R4 `procedure` if the case information must be preserved, because R4 requires `procedure.type` whenever `procedure` exists.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Rename `procedure` to `case`, `procedure.identifier` to `case.identifier`, `procedure.type` to `case.type`, `procedure.date[x]` to `case.date[x]`, and recursive `procedure.application` to `case.application`. For reverse conversion, require a case type or define a local placeholder policy, and decide how to handle multiple identifiers and case status.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The breaking rename was avoidable by retaining `procedure` as a deprecated alias. R6 likely chose a more general term that better fits applications and cases across regulatory domains.

freshReview.narrativeMd: `procedure` is renamed to `case`, and several child rules are broadened: identifiers become repeatable, `type` is no longer required, and `status` is added. The old field name is a real wire/codegen break, but forward migration is usually a direct structural rename with compatible child datatypes. Given the R4 artifact's FMM 0 status and the R6 note that this area is still seeking implementer feedback, the broader `case` terminology seems proportionate even though a less-breaking name-retention design was available.
keyEvidence: R4 `procedure` is 0..1 BackboneElement with `identifier` 0..1, required `type` 1..1, `date[x]` Period/dateTime, and recursive `application`.
R6 `case` is 0..1 BackboneElement with `identifier` 0..*, `type` 0..1, `status` 0..1, same `date[x]` choice, and recursive `application`.
R6 `case` definition describes the case or regulatory procedure and notes ongoing workgroup review/implementer feedback.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 0/trial-use softens the concern over a path rename. The path is audit/workflow relevant, but the forward transform is mechanical and the R6 design goal is understandable.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: the old `procedure` property is not valid on R6 `RegulatedAuthorization`; R6-to-R4 loss can occur for `case.status`, multiple identifiers, or cases without a type.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Yes but with modest benefit. R6 could have kept the `procedure` name and broadened its definition/children, avoiding the wire break. The tradeoff is retaining a less general name for a broader administrative case model.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree: the existing report correctly identifies an avoidable rename, but the low maturity and straightforward migration make the final judgment `Breaking but probably OK` rather than `Revisit`.

findings.title: status becomes an R6 modifier element with a preferred publication-status binding

oldState.summary: Optional CodeableConcept status, not a modifier, no local binding.

semanticText.definition: The status of the marketing authorization.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 status was summary data but not flagged as a modifier.

newState.summary: Optional CodeableConcept status, isModifier true, preferred binding to publication-status.

binding.description: The lifecycle status of an artifact.

flags.isModifierReason: This element is labelled as a modifier because it is a status element that can indicate that a record should not be treated as valid

semanticText.definition: The status that is authorised e.g. approved. Intermediate states and actions can be tracked with cases and applications.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 status is a modifier because it can indicate the record should not be treated as valid.

facts.oldValue: The status of the marketing authorization.
facts.newValue: The status that is authorised e.g. approved. Intermediate states and actions can be tracked with cases and applications.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The cardinality and data type do not create a direct old-valid/new-invalid validation break, and the binding is only preferred. However, `isModifier=true` changes safe-processing obligations: consumers must inspect `status` before treating the authorization as valid/current. Generated models, serializers, and business rules that previously ignored status can become unsafe in R6.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Ignoring a status that indicates invalid, inactive, or non-current authorization can lead to use of a product authorization that should not be relied on.

justification.inferredGoal: Make lifecycle status a safe-processing modifier for generalized authorizations.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep `status` non-modifier and rely on warning invariants, best-practice guidance, or profiles to require status-aware processing.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: This is not a structural old-valid/new-invalid instance break, but it is a real runtime and safe-processing change. The R6 modifier reason states that status can indicate a record should not be treated as valid, which is important for regulatory authorization use. A warning-only approach would be less breaking but would not provide the same base-level machine-readable obligation, so the modifier change is probably justified.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A softer base design could have left `status` as a normal element and added best-practice warnings, examples, or profile constraints telling consumers to inspect it. That would preserve old client assumptions better, but it would also allow generic processors to ignore status in situations where inactive, invalid, or non-current authorization status changes the meaning of the record. The alternative is therefore only partial.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Less disruptive for clients, but weaker as a machine-readable safety signal because consumers can still ignore status.

evidence.detail: R4 status is a CodeableConcept with isModifier false and no local binding.
R6 status is a CodeableConcept with isModifier true and a preferred publication-status binding.

examples.examplesMd: The example shows aligning a status coding with the preferred R6 publication-status binding when local semantics permit.

findings.narrativeMd: `status` remains optional and still uses `CodeableConcept`, but its processing role changes. In R6, systems cannot safely ignore it because it is a modifier element.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: This is mostly a runtime/conformance break, not a strict instance validation break. Existing status codings may still validate because the binding is preferred, but R6 clients, validators, and generated code can treat the element differently because of the modifier flag.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Review all code paths that display, exchange, or act on authorizations. Ensure status is parsed and considered before treating an authorization as usable. Where feasible, map local statuses to publication-status or preserve local codings with clear text and business rules.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: A softer alternative would have been best-practice guidance or warnings, but that would not force consumers to inspect status. The modifier flag is a reasonable safety-oriented change, though it raises implementation obligations.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: Confirm local status vocabularies before mapping to publication-status; marketing authorization statuses may not align one-to-one with publication lifecycle statuses.

freshReview.narrativeMd: `status` keeps the same cardinality and CodeableConcept type but becomes an R6 modifier with a preferred publication-status binding. This is not an old-valid/new-invalid structural break because the binding is preferred, but it changes safe-processing obligations: consumers should inspect status before treating an authorization as usable. That is a meaningful runtime/codegen concern, yet the modifier reason is directly tied to preventing invalid or non-current authorization records from being treated as valid, so a softer warning-only design would weaken the safety signal.
keyEvidence: R4 `status` is 0..1 CodeableConcept, summary, and not a modifier.
R6 `status` is 0..1 CodeableConcept, summary, `isModifier=true`, with reason that status can indicate a record should not be treated as valid.
R6 `status` binding to publication-status is preferred, not required.
freshReview.fmmEffect: Low R4 FMM reduces the compatibility burden, but status is central to safe regulatory use. The modifier flag is a proportionate base-level signal rather than an avoidable cosmetic change.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: runtime/API/codegen: generated models, validators, and consumers may treat `status` as a modifier that must be checked; there is no hard instance break from the preferred binding alone.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Partial. R6 could have left `status` non-modifier and used guidance or warning-level conformance, but that would not provide the same machine-readable obligation to avoid relying on invalid authorizations.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree with the existing assessment that this is primarily runtime risk, not a hard validation break, and that the less-breaking alternative is only partial.

findings.title: legalBasis is renamed and broadened to repeatable basis with an example binding

oldState.summary: Optional single CodeableConcept legal basis without local binding.

semanticText.definition: The legal framework against which this authorization is granted.

newState.summary: Optional repeatable CodeableConcept basis with example regulated-authorization-basis binding.

binding.description: A legal or regulatory framework against which an authorization is granted, or other reasons for it.

semanticText.definition: The legal or regulatory framework against which this authorization is granted, or other reasons for it.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 `basis` broadens the concept to legal, regulatory, or other reasons and permits multiple values.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The definitions both cover the legal/regulatory framework against which authorization is granted.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The old `legalBasis` field name is invalid in R6, so R4 instances need transformation. Forward conversion is usually straightforward by moving the concept to `basis`; reverse conversion can be lossy because R6 allows multiple bases and non-legal reasons.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: The legal or regulatory basis can affect permitted use and compliance interpretation.

justification.inferredGoal: Broaden legal basis into a generalized authorization basis.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain `legalBasis` while broadening its definition, cardinality, and example binding to cover generalized authorization bases.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Broadening the concept from a single legal framework to one or more authorization bases is reasonable. The breaking part is the rename to `basis`, and the calibration rules explicitly recognize that living with a nonoptimal R4 name can be a valid compatibility strategy. R6 could have kept `legalBasis` with an updated definition and repeatable cardinality, so the field-name break was probably avoidable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best less-breaking base design would keep `legalBasis` as the element name, change its max to `*`, and define it as the legal, regulatory, or other basis for the authorization. That preserves all R4 instances and supports the new broader semantics without adding a parallel `basis` field. The main cost is terminology awkwardness when the basis is not strictly legal.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: The retained name is less precise for non-legal reasons, but avoids duplicate basis fields and preserves old payloads.

evidence.detail: R4 defines legalBasis as 0..1 CodeableConcept.
R6 defines basis as 0..* CodeableConcept with an example regulated-authorization-basis binding.
The local R6 CodeSystem includes basis concepts such as Full, NewSubstance, KnownSubstance, SimilarBiological, TemporaryUse, and ParallelTrade.

examples.examplesMd: The old-valid/new-invalid example assumes the resource has been renamed but the old property name was not.

findings.narrativeMd: `legalBasis` is not preserved as a field name. R6 uses a broader and repeatable `basis` element, with example terminology for authorization bases.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4-derived R6 payload that still contains `legalBasis` is invalid. R6 `basis` values can be mapped back to R4 only if at most one basis is present and local policy treats it as a legal framework rather than some other reason.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Map `legalBasis` to a single-item `basis` array. For reverse conversion, reject or extension-map multiple bases unless a local rule can combine them. Consider mapping local legal-basis codes to the R6 example CodeSystem when appropriate, but do not force a lossy code translation.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The rename and broadening could have been introduced compatibly by retaining the old field as deprecated. The R6 design reduces medicinal-specific naming in favor of a general authorization concept.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 `legalBasis` becomes repeatable `basis`, broadening from a single legal framework to legal, regulatory, or other authorization reasons. The cardinality broadening and example binding are not the issue; the avoidable break is the field rename. Legal or regulatory basis is an audit/compliance-relevant concept, and R6 could likely have kept the old wire name while broadening its definition and max cardinality. The new shorter name is cleaner for non-legal reasons, but the compatibility cost seems disproportionate for an optional CodeableConcept path.
keyEvidence: R4 `legalBasis` is 0..1 CodeableConcept with definition `The legal framework against which this authorization is granted.`
R6 `basis` is 0..* CodeableConcept with definition covering legal/regulatory framework or other reasons.
R6 `basis` binding is example strength, so terminology does not create a hard validation break.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 0/trial-use softens the stability concern, but legal/regulatory basis is compliance and audit relevant, and the less-breaking base design is low cost enough to justify `Revisit`.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: old `legalBasis` is not a valid R6 property; R6-to-R4 loss can occur for multiple bases or non-legal reasons.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Yes. R6 could have kept `legalBasis`, made it repeatable, and broadened its definition. The tradeoff is an imperfect name for non-legal reasons, but it avoids duplicate fields and preserves old payloads.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree with the existing medium-impact and less-breaking-available assessment; the fresh review treats this as an avoidable compliance-relevant rename.

findings.title: R6 adds generalized authorization content with no clean R4 representation

affectedLocation.newPath: RegulatedAuthorization.type / description / indication / intendedUse / attachedDocument / case.status

oldState.summary: R4 has no direct local elements for overall authorization type, description, indication, intended use, attached documents, or procedure status.
oldState.narrativeMd: The R4 resource was narrower and did not include these generalized R6 fields.

newState.summary: R6 adds type, description, indication, intendedUse, attachedDocument, and case.status.

binding.description: New fields use example or preferred bindings, including regulated-authorization-type, product-intended-use, and publication-status.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 `RegulatedAuthorization` includes additional optional content that supports broader authorization scenarios.

facts.newValue: All listed R6 elements are optional.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Optional additions do not make old R4 instances invalid when migrating forward, but they matter for reverse conversion and round-trip tooling. R6 instances using these elements cannot be serialized into R4 without extensions, contained documents, lossy omission, or manual mapping.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Attached documents, indication, intended use, and case status can carry regulatory evidence and workflow state.

justification.inferredGoal: Add expressiveness needed by a generalized regulated authorization resource.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable because the listed R6 elements are optional additions and do not create an R4-to-R6 base validation break.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Adding optional `RegulatedAuthorization` content for type, description, indication, intended use, attached documents, and case status is a reasonable way to increase R6 expressiveness without invalidating R4-derived instances. The compatibility concern is R6-to-R4 representability, not a breaking R4-to-R6 base-design choice, so the change is justified in the forward direction.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Because the additions are optional, R4 instances can migrate forward without supplying them. There is no base R6 alternative that makes native R4 capable of representing concepts it never defined; extension preservation, down-conversion rules, or lossy omission are conversion mitigations rather than backward-compatible R6 base-design alternatives.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: No less-breaking R6 base design is needed for forward compatibility; R4 down-conversion remains inherently lossy without extensions or policy.

evidence.detail: R6 defines optional added elements not present in the R4 MedicinalProductAuthorization differential.
R4 has no corresponding local elements for the listed additions.

examples.examplesMd: R4 could carry this information only through extensions, related resources, or local conventions.

findings.narrativeMd: The R6 successor is not merely a renamed R4 resource; it adds new optional content for authorization type, supporting narrative, indications, intended use, documents, and case status. These additions are useful in R6 but create round-trip risk.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Because the additions are optional, they do not break R4-to-R6 validation. They are R6-valid but not R4-representable without extensions or lossy omission.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: When down-converting R6 to R4, decide which R6-only fields are dropped, extension-mapped, or represented through linked resources. Round-trip tests should assert whether extension preservation is required.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Optional additions are the least disruptive way to add expressiveness in the forward direction. The remaining incompatibility is unavoidable for native R4 representation, so the main need is official or local conversion guidance.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: This finding is primarily for systems that must support bidirectional R4/R6 conversion or long-term mixed-version archives.

freshReview.narrativeMd: The listed R6-only elements (`type`, `description`, `indication`, `intendedUse`, `attachedDocument`, and `case.status`) are optional additions. They do not make R4-derived content invalid in the forward R4-to-R6 direction, and native R4 could not represent these concepts without extensions or local conventions anyway. They matter for down-conversion and round-trip tooling, but that is not a reason to question the R6 base design.
keyEvidence: R6 `RegulatedAuthorization` defines optional `type`, `description`, `indication`, `intendedUse`, `attachedDocument`, and `case.status` elements.
R4 `MedicinalProductAuthorization` has no direct local counterparts for those fields.
The new R6 bindings observed for these additions are example or preferred, not required.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 0/trial-use further lowers concern because the finding is reverse-conversion only. No broad production impact should be inferred from optional R6 additions.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss: R6 instances using these optional additions may not down-convert losslessly to native R4, but there is no meaningful R4-to-R6 break.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Not applicable. Optional R6 additions are already the least disruptive forward-compatible design; R4 down-conversion requires extensions or policy outside the R6 base model.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: disagree with the existing medium-impact framing for this review purpose: the reverse-conversion limitation is real, but as an R4-to-R6 compatibility finding it is not a problem.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: No local non-inherited invariants on `MedicinalProductAuthorization` or `RegulatedAuthorization` were found beyond inherited base/BackboneElement constraints, which are out of scope.
No local fixed, pattern, or default value constraints were identified on the compared local elements.
No local maxLength, regex, minValue, or maxValue restrictions were identified for the compared artifact-specific elements.
No local slicing rules were present on the compared artifact-specific content.

Comparable scalar and backbone mappings retain the same broad datatypes where a clear counterpart exists: Identifier, CodeableConcept, Period, dateTime, and Organization references. Material reference target and element-presence changes are reported separately.

No local counterpart showed an R4-to-R6 minimum increase or maximum decrease. Some mapped elements are broadened, such as `subject` 0..1 to 0..*, `legalBasis` 0..1 to `basis` 0..*, and `procedure.type` 1..1 to `case.type` 0..1. Removed fields are handled as element-presence findings.
Comparable local business elements remain summary elements. Inherited/base summary flag changes, if any, are out of scope.

No primitive wire-format change was found for retained choice values such as `procedure.date[x]` to `case.date[x]`, which both support Period and dateTime. Major serialization impact is due to resource and element renaming, which is covered in findings.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: The inferred R6 successor is active while the R4 resource was draft
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: Standards status is not an instance validation rule for old payloads by itself.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: The status change suggests the R6 model may be more mature, but it does not reduce the need for explicit resource and element migration.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.path: RegulatedAuthorization.type / region / basis / intendedUse / case.type / case.status
nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: R6 adds example or preferred bindings to several local elements
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The bindings observed on these elements are `example` or `preferred`, not `required`, so they do not by themselves make old CodeableConcept codings invalid.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Terminology-aware implementations should review the new R6 ValueSets and CodeSystems to improve semantic alignment, especially for authorization type, basis, and case type.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Resource definition broadens from medicinal product authorization to regulated authorization
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The broader definition is already represented by the artifact-identity and subject findings; as text alone it does not create an additional validation rule.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Profiles may be needed if an implementation wants to preserve the narrower R4 medicinal-product-only semantics on top of R6 `RegulatedAuthorization`.

analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Terminology server expansions and mapping tables for local regulatory code systems would clarify conformance risk.
